facts.statement: The genus contains only one species, Z. zangjiazhuangensis, which was named in 2017 based on a single humerus.

facts.statement: The animal is known from a single humerus discovered in the Wangshi Group near Zhucheng, Shandong, China.

facts.statement: Researchers uncovered the humerus and other sauropod bones at the Zangjiazhuang Quarry in 2008.

facts.statement: The humerus was catalogued with the number ZJZ-57.

facts.statement: The top end of the humerus is 0.55 times the length of the entire bone, a proportion extreme compared to other titanosaurs.

facts.statement: The extreme width of the humerus top end arises because the inner edge angles more sharply inwards there than at the bottom.

facts.statement: The prominent deltopectoral crest bears a hook-like process extending about halfway down its length.

facts.statement: The deltopectoral crest extends down to the midshaft and sideways to occupy the outer width of the bone.
facts.quote: It extends downwards to the midshaft of the bone, and sideways so that it occupies the outer of the bone's width.

facts.statement: Mo and colleagues assigned Zhuchengtitan to the family Saltasauridae based on specific humeral traits.

facts.statement: Dating of a basalt layer places the Hongtuya Member at 73.5 million years old, corresponding to the Campanian age of the Cretaceous.
facts.quote: Based on argon-argon dating of the basalt layer at its top end, the Hongtuya Member at Zangjiazhuang has been estimated at 73.5 Ma in age, which places it during the Campanian age of the Cretaceous period.

facts.statement: Zhuchengtitan lived at the end of the Cretaceous period, approximately 72 million years ago, during the Maastrichtian.

facts.statement: The genus name Zhuchengtitan combines the location Zhucheng with the Greek suffix titan.
